section_summary: This section documents U.S. and British efforts in early 1941 to limit Japan’s accumulation of petroleum and other strategic materials, especially through tanker control, export licensing, and restrictions on oil drums and storage tanks. It also covers exports of aluminum, fats, bearings, jute bags, asbestos, lard, and toluol, alongside correspondence urging a broader embargo against Japan. The final documents report German machinery and military-related goods entering Manchuria and provide intelligence on Japan’s severe asbestos shortage.

subfiles.title: Universal Oil Products cover letter concerning the Japan Gasoline Company
subfiles.from: S. R. Wilson, Universal Oil Products Company
subfiles.to: H. W. Moseley, Division of Controls, Department of State
subfiles.about: Transmits R. L. Gilpatric’s January 21 letter about the Japan Gasoline Company.
subfiles.summary: Wilson forwards Gilpatric's letter at Hiram Halle's request; Halle read it to Moseley by telephone that morning.

subfiles.title: Gilpatric letter on settlement terms in the Japan Gasoline dispute
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese proposal limiting requests for gasoline-process information in exchange for suspending litigation.
subfiles.summary: Yamaoka reports Saneyoshi would forgo iso-octane data, limit requests to ordinary motor-fuel processes, and suspend the litigation for two years if Universal and State accept.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Louis E. Berry’s activities in Japan
subfiles.about: Points to a report concerning metallurgical expert Louis E. Berry’s activities in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references a Justice Department letter transmitting a report on Louis E. Berry. The original was filed under 894.00/1001.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Ambassador Nomura’s embargo warning
subfiles.about: References a memorandum reporting Nomura’s warning about the consequences of continued American embargoes.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Ambassador Nomura told Hull Japan's military might feel forced toward further action if American embargoes continue.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on limiting rubber exports to Japan
subfiles.about: References a telegram about a regional arrangement limiting rubber exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Indochina, the East Indies and Malaya were arranging to limit rubber exports to Japan's home-consumption requirements.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference concerning transactions involving Prieto
subfiles.about: References another file concerning sales or proposals involving a person named Prieto.
subfiles.summary: Largely illegible cross-reference apparently about sales or proposals to Ruben Prieto, directing to another file.

subfiles.title: Telegram on aluminum tanks being shipped from Manzanillo to Dairen
subfiles.about: Reports plans to break up four aluminum tanks for shipment to Dairen.
subfiles.summary: Four large aluminum tanks at Manzanillo are being cut up for shipment to Dairen, Manchukuo, yielding six tons of aluminum, shipped by La Consolidada.

subfiles.title: Message about a Richfield Oil Company meeting with the Secretary of State
subfiles.from: Mr. Brown, Office of the Secretary
subfiles.about: Requests preparation of a memorandum for a meeting on petroleum exports to the Far East.
subfiles.summary: At Colonel Hurley's instance Richfield Oil president Charles Jones will see the Secretary January 14, probably on Far East petroleum exports; a briefing memorandum is requested.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation on Japanese oil stocks, quotas, and tankers
subfiles.about: Records British proposals to restrict Japan’s oil reserves by controlling quotas and tanker availability.
subfiles.summary: Neville Butler and P. C. Hill urged U.S. cooperation in discouraging Standard-Vacuum from accepting increased Japanese quotas and using its foreign-flag tankers in the Japan trade. Hornbeck obtained figures showing Standard’s proposed quota totaled 99,200 tons and that it used only two tankers between Japan and the Netherlands East Indies. He stressed the delicacy of petroleum restrictions and recalled earlier British and Dutch warnings about provoking damaging repercussions. An addendum records Hill’s estimate that Shell’s increased quota was about 140,000 tons.

subfiles.title: Handwritten calculations of Standard-Vacuum’s Japanese quota
subfiles.about: Calculates petroleum-product figures associated with Standard-Vacuum’s proposed Japanese quota.
subfiles.summary: Handwritten calculations totaling Standard-Vacuum's Japanese quota of gasoline, kerosene and heavy oils at 99,200 tons.

subfiles.title: British memorandum titled “Oil—Japan”
subfiles.about: Urges prompt agreement on restricting Japanese oil imports through tanker control.
subfiles.summary: British memorandum "Oil-Japan": larger Japanese quotas for Standard and Shell would need more tanker tonnage, enlarge Japan's oil intake and undermine their China marketing; Britain needs a prompt State decision on tanker curtailment.

subfiles.title: Table of U.S. petroleum-product exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Compares monthly U.S. petroleum exports to Japan in 1939 and August–November 1940.
subfiles.summary: Table of U.S. petroleum-product exports to Japan, showing large 1940 increases in non-aviation gasoline and lubricating oil.

subfiles.title: Table of Japanese petroleum imports
subfiles.about: Presents Japanese petroleum-import totals and the effect of the Batavia agreement.
subfiles.summary: Table of Japanese petroleum imports in prewar years; the Batavia agreement gives 1.8 million tons yearly, 42.4 percent of 1939 imports.

subfiles.title: Instruction on licensing metal drums and liquid containers
subfiles.to: Collector of Customs, New York, and other collectors
subfiles.about: Explains which metal drums and containers were exempt from or subject to export licensing.
subfiles.summary: Instruction exempts small and some intermediate containers from the February 4 iron-and-steel export order; other liquid containers need licenses after February 15, and petroleum licenses don't cover their drums.

subfiles.title: British Embassy letter advocating tanker restrictions
subfiles.about: Urges U.S. action against American-owned foreign-flag tankers and increased oil deliveries to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Butler encloses data on Panamanian and Philippine tankers to Japan, argues restricting Japanese chartering would curb stock accumulation, asks that Standard Oil be discouraged from larger quotas, and suggests licensing drum exports.

subfiles.title: List of tanker sailings to Japan from U.S. ports
subfiles.about: Lists November and December tanker departures for Japan and their owners.
subfiles.summary: List of eight Panamanian and one Philippine tankers leaving Philadelphia and New York for Japan, separating U.S.-linked vessels from Norwegian or Greek ones.

subfiles.title: British Embassy letter on Japanese purchases of oil-storage tanks
subfiles.about: Warns that Japan was rapidly expanding permanent oil-storage capacity with tanks imported from the United States.
subfiles.summary: Butler estimates tanks shipped since December 1 supplied about two million barrels of capacity, plus one million in October-November, suggesting Japanese reserve building; he asks about restricting structural-steel tanks.

subfiles.title: List of oil-storage tank shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Lists major steel storage tanks shipped from U.S. Pacific ports since December 1, 1940.
subfiles.summary: List of oil-storage tank shipments on five Japanese vessels totaling about 1,957,000 barrels, including tanks at Qingdao.

subfiles.title: Maritime Commission consultation on foreign tanker chartering
subfiles.about: Reports that Maritime Commission officials might discourage American owners from chartering foreign-flag tankers to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Maritime Commission's Robeson and Wilcox think an arrangement with American tanker owners may be possible and request State's interest first.

subfiles.title: Cover memorandum to Welles on withdrawing tankers from Japanese use
subfiles.about: Forwards a proposal for informal approaches to oil companies controlling tankers used in the Japan trade.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs recommends asking oil companies voluntarily to find non-Japanese cargoes for tankers.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on tanker shipments of petroleum products to Japan
subfiles.about: Recommends confidential approaches to American oil companies controlling foreign-flag tankers.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum counts 388 American-flag and 217 American-controlled foreign-flag tankers, names seven likely companies and proposes asking them for alternative employment; joint withholding would hinder Japan with less resentment than a direct ban.

subfiles.title: International Communications comments on gaps in tanker restrictions
subfiles.from: Thomas Burke, Division of International Communications
subfiles.about: Notes that voluntary tanker controls would not fully restrict Japanese oil imports.
subfiles.summary: Burke concurs but notes companies could use their own uncontrolled tankers, suggests restricting drummed gasoline and lubricants on cargo ships, and warns owners may resist leaving the safe Japan trade.

subfiles.title: Duplicate memorandum on gaps in proposed tanker restrictions
subfiles.from: Thomas Burke, Division of International Communications
subfiles.about: Duplicate copy of the memorandum assessing weaknesses in proposed tanker controls.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate of Burke's memorandum on gaps in tanker restrictions: company-owned tankers, drummed cargo and owners' preference for safe Japanese employment.

subfiles.title: Feis routing note requesting a reply to Clayton
subfiles.about: Requests a draft reply explaining how a matter raised by Clayton would be handled in a prospective export-control order.
subfiles.summary: Feis asks that a reply to William Clayton be prepared for his signature on how the pending order will address the products.

subfiles.title: Inquiry to Yost about withheld export licenses
subfiles.about: Asks why licenses for specified exports to Japan were not being issued and whether normal-quantity limits had been considered.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs asks Yost why licenses on listed commodities were withheld and whether the normal-quantity formula could replace complete refusal.

subfiles.title: Clayton letter on exports of fats to Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards a memorandum about fats exported to Japan and questions whether they might be reaching Germany.
subfiles.summary: Clayton sends Feis a February 26 memorandum, speculating exported fats might be moving through Japan to Germany.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on exports of oils and fats to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports large shipments of coconut oil, salad oil, and lard to Japan.
subfiles.summary: C. E. Lund reports exports of about eighteen million pounds of coconut oil and 400,000 of salad oil, with seven million pounds of lard awaiting loading; Groggins questions the final use of animal oils, not normally in the Japanese diet.

subfiles.title: Feis reply to Clayton on controls over fats and oils
subfiles.about: Explains new and prospective export controls on oils and fats destined for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Feis states that coconut oil, copra, palm oil, palm kernels, and vegetable-oil fatty acids became subject to licensing on March 10. No licenses were being issued for their export to Japan. He adds that the Department had recommended controls on remaining fats and oils and expected further action shortly.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Herron’s call about lubricating oil in wooden barrels
subfiles.about: Records information that Japanese buyers were seeking lubricating oil packed in new oak barrels.
subfiles.summary: California Texas Oil president Herron says brokers nationwide are asked to ship lubricating oil in wooden barrels; his company refused to quote on 22,000 barrels.

subfiles.title: Timken letter announcing refusal of Japanese and Russian bearing orders
subfiles.about: Explains Timken’s decision to stop bearing sales to Japan and Russia.
subfiles.summary: Timken, without government guidance, refused new Japanese inquiries, canceled $250,000 of Japanese and $26,984 of Russian orders, and barred future sales, seeing bearings as indirect nickel exports aiding munitions.

subfiles.title: Division of Controls memorandum recording Campbell’s visit
subfiles.about: Records A. F. Campbell’s delivery of Timken’s statement on export policy.
subfiles.summary: Campbell left Timken's letter to record its export attitude; Exton understood copies went to Colonel MacMorland and Commander Harrison.

subfiles.title: Timken confirmation that sales to Japan and Russia had stopped
subfiles.from: W. E. Umstattd, Timken Roller Bearing Company
subfiles.about: Confirms that Timken had ordered an end to shipments to Japanese and Russian customers.
subfiles.summary: Umstattd says Timken weighed defense implications and on March 10 told sales departments to stop all sales and shipments to Japanese and Russian customers.

subfiles.title: Schober letter protesting Philippine exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Urges action against shipments from the Philippine Islands to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Schober cites Woodbury Willoughby that the President's export order didn't bar certain Philippine shipments to Japan and asks Welles to stop the traffic.

subfiles.title: Reply explaining that the Export Control Act did not apply to the Philippines
subfiles.from: Department of State, by direction of Sumner Welles
subfiles.about: Explains the statutory limits on applying U.S. export controls to the Philippine Islands.
subfiles.summary: State explains the July 2, 1940 Export Control Act applied to exports from the U.S. but not the Philippines, and new legislation would be needed to extend it.

subfiles.title: Green memorandum on proposed jute-bag shipments
subfiles.about: Records General Maxwell’s decision not to stop imminent jute-bag shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Green and General Maxwell discuss British reports of jute exports; Maxwell finds jute-bag supplies not scarce, and jute comes under export control March 24.

subfiles.title: Yost memorandum reporting British figures for jute shipments
subfiles.about: Reports quantities of jute bags being loaded for Japan at four U.S. ports.
subfiles.summary: Yost reports British consular figures for jute shipments: 485 tons at Seattle, 645 at San Francisco, 150 at Portland, 3,454 bales at New Orleans; the Waste Bag Dealers Association feared U.S. shortage.

subfiles.title: Welles routing note assigning the Fuller letter
subfiles.about: Directs Hamilton to answer Henry M. Fuller’s protest letter.
subfiles.summary: Welles refers the incoming correspondence to Hamilton. He asks Hamilton to prepare the Department’s response.

subfiles.title: Fuller letter protesting arms and strategic exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Urges an embargo on materials that could support Japan’s war effort.
subfiles.summary: Fuller condemns continued exports of cotton, scrap, metals, gasoline and aircraft materials to Japan, citing Senators Tobey, White and Bridges, and asks Welles to press for an embargo.

subfiles.title: Hamilton reply to Fuller on export-control policy
subfiles.about: Explains the legal and administrative basis of U.S. export controls.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton describes the Export Control Act's authority, says the Administrator decides with agency advice, and assures Fuller conditions are continually reviewed.

subfiles.title: Philadelphia Customs report on abnormal lard shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: G. S. Peffall, Assistant Collector of Customs, Philadelphia
subfiles.about: Reports more than 1.2 million pounds of refined lard booked for Yokohama.
subfiles.summary: Philadelphia Customs reports 15,135 crates and 300 barrels of lard, from Cudahy for Mitsubishi Shoji, loading on the Nako Maru for Yokohama, flagged as abnormal.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment of the Philadelphia Customs report
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Thanks Customs for reporting abnormal exports and requests similar future information.
subfiles.summary: State says the reported shipments are receiving appropriate consideration and asks the collector to keep reporting unusual Philadelphia exports.

subfiles.title: Transmission of the Philadelphia lard report to the Export Control Administrator
subfiles.about: Forwards the Customs report on abnormal shipments destined for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Green sends the Export Control Administrator the Philadelphia collector's March 20 letter on abnormal lard shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: Export Control Administrator’s acknowledgment of the Philadelphia report
subfiles.from: Russell L. Maxwell, Administrator of Export Control
subfiles.to: Chief, Division of Controls, Department of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of the report on Philadelphia shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Maxwell thanks the Division of Controls for forwarding the Philadelphia collector’s March 20 report. The document identifies the subject simply as shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: Confidential letter to the Maritime Commission on tanker employment
subfiles.from: Breckinridge Long, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Suggests redirecting American-owned foreign-flag tankers toward trades serving U.S. defense needs.
subfiles.summary: The Department notes a global shortage of tanker tonnage and an apparently excessive use of American-controlled foreign-flag tankers in Pacific trade. It asks the Maritime Commission to consider influencing their employment toward national-defense needs. Any approaches to owners were to remain strictly confidential, informal, and oral.

subfiles.title: Bayard Clark letter asking about gasoline shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Requests clarification of reports that American gasoline sent to Japan was reaching Germany through Russia.
subfiles.summary: Bayard Clark reports North Carolina talk of large gasoline sales to Japan, allegedly passing through Russia to Germany, and asks Hull about policy and the diversion claim.

subfiles.title: Hull reply to Clark on gasoline export controls
subfiles.about: Assures Clark that controlled gasoline exports harmful to national defense were not being licensed.
subfiles.summary: Hull cites Section 6 of the July 2, 1940 act, declines a fixed policy since controls keep changing, and assures Clark controlled products including gasoline aren't permitted when detrimental to defense.

subfiles.title: Inter-office memorandum on asbestos supplies in Japan
subfiles.about: Recommends obtaining field intelligence on Japan’s asbestos supplies and stockpiles.
subfiles.summary: Memorandum: Japan imports substantial crude asbestos, mostly from Canada; Leonard recommends asking foreign representatives about shortages and stockpiles.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Tokyo requesting asbestos information
subfiles.about: Requests discreet information about Japanese asbestos supplies and shortages.
subfiles.summary: Instruction asks the Tokyo Embassy to discreetly obtain information on asbestos supply sources and shortages.

subfiles.title: Johnson memorandum on Canadian asbestos restrictions
subfiles.about: Reports Canadian quotas and licensing restrictions on asbestos exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Johnson favors a cable to Tokyo; Canada limited asbestos exports to Japan to half the five-year level and refused top grades, though U.S. exports and differing definitions may weaken the controls.

subfiles.title: Grew telegram on Japan’s asbestos shortage
subfiles.about: Reports very low Japanese stocks of crude asbestos, particularly military grades.
subfiles.summary: Grew: Japan holds about 5,000-7,000 tons of crude asbestos, two or three months' supply, after importing 23,300 tons in 1940; Canada restricts fine grades, and the Army took all long-fiber stocks.

subfiles.title: Yost transmission of asbestos intelligence to Export Control
subfiles.about: Forwards the Tokyo Embassy’s asbestos report and a Canadian note on export policy.
subfiles.summary: Yost sends Sanger of the Planning Division a paraphrase of Grew's telegram and a Canadian note on asbestos exports to the Far East.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Grew’s asbestos telegram
subfiles.about: File copy paraphrasing the Embassy’s report on Japan’s asbestos stocks and sources.
subfiles.summary: The paraphrase estimates Japanese crude-asbestos stocks at 5,000–7,000 tons and 1940 imports at 23,300 tons, chiefly from Canada. It reports Canadian licensing restrictions, Army seizure of long-fiber stocks, negligible yen-bloc production, and transport barriers to supplies from Rhodesia, South Africa, and Mozambique. A more detailed despatch was being prepared.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference concerning mining interests and ore deposits
subfiles.about: References a memorandum concerning a mining company and ore deposits in the Philippines.
subfiles.summary: Largely obscured cross-reference apparently about Chrome or Iron Mines, Inc. and ore deposits, filed at 811b.6351/10.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Senator Morris Sheppard’s letter on shipments
subfiles.about: References a letter concerning shipments that might fall under export restrictions.
subfiles.summary: Degraded cross-reference to Senator Morris Sheppard's letter on shipments, filed at 861.24/467.

subfiles.title: Despatch on toluol aboard the scuttled Atlas
subfiles.from: Josephus Daniels, U.S. Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Reports the condition and likely disposition of toluol aboard the Italian ship Atlas at Tampico.
subfiles.summary: Toluol aboard the Atlas, scuttled April 1, was probably undamaged; purchase is difficult because Mexico wants it for its TNT factory, where it would probably go if Mexico takes the cargo.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Mexico City regarding aluminum intended for Dairen
subfiles.about: Directs efforts to keep six tons of aluminum in Mexico instead of allowing shipment to Dairen.
subfiles.summary: Embassy is asked to urge Mexico's Foreign Office and La Consolidada's American officials to use the Dairen-bound aluminum within Mexico, citing U.S. efforts to supply aluminum to Mexico's War Department.

subfiles.title: Shipstead letter forwarding a constituent’s protest over exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards Mrs. Samuel Gilmore Dickinson’s letter and requests a report on exports of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Shipstead forwards Dickinson's protest on scrap, oil and other materials sold to Japan, asking Hull for a report and the letter's return.

subfiles.title: Dickinson letter demanding an end to war-material exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Calls for an immediate halt to exports of scrap iron, oil, and other war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Dickinson argues supplying Japan arms a probable enemy, compares inaction to Britain and France at Hitler's Rhineland move, and favors accepting a smaller conflict now rather than a stronger Japan later.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator Shipstead on war-material exports
subfiles.about: Explains licensing controls over scrap iron, petroleum products, and other strategic exports.
subfiles.summary: The reply states that iron and steel scrap, aviation fuel, lubricants, and many other products required special export licenses. Licenses were denied whenever a proposed export was considered detrimental to national defense. It adds that controls were continually revised and extended to new commodities as conditions changed.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram on German goods entering Manchuria
subfiles.about: Lists German industrial and military-related equipment recently delivered to Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Tokyo telegram: German goods for Manchuria, January-March 1941, include locomotives, Heinkel and Junkers aircraft, torpedo speedboats, trucks and factory machinery; routed via Shanghai and circulated to military intelligence.
